prize_parts.citation: For the development of halide perovskites as solution-processed absorbers for high-efficiency solar cells

statement.case_for: Halide perovskites are a new semiconductor family whose chemistry (composition, crystallisation, defect tolerance, ion mobility) was worked out in a single decade, taking solar-cell efficiency from a few percent to above 25 percent and spilling over into LEDs and detectors. The priority sequence is traceable: Miyasaka's first perovskite sensitiser cell (2009), Park's solid-state cell and Snaith's meso-superstructured and planar devices (2012) turned a curiosity into a thin-film technology. The efficiency records have been reproduced in laboratories worldwide, so the central scientific picture is no longer in doubt. This is materials chemistry with direct bearing on the energy transition, which is what the prize was meant to reward.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the real weakness: six credited names, a three-person limit, and Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis all have strong claims, while Kojima, who was on the 2009 paper, is not even in the credited list. Stability, lead toxicity and commercial durability are unresolved, and several colleagues rank it low, with only Linke and Aili placing it in their top five. If the committee judges that no fair three-person split exists, the field should wait or be dropped in favour of a cleaner case.

responses.point: Perovskite solar cells may be premature because long-term stability, lead toxicity and commercial viability remain open, and credit is dispersed among six names.
responses.response: I accept the attribution concern and cannot fully answer it, but I do not think stability makes the discovery premature. We do not ask whether a discovery has reached the market. We ask whether the finding is confirmed and has changed a field. Efficiency has been reproduced independently and the compositional and defect chemistry is now a large literature. Silicon and lithium-ion batteries were also recognised before their engineering problems were settled. I would rather see Car-Parrinello as an equally mature alternative than treat perovskites as unripe, but I do not see B061 as clearly stronger on impact beyond the simulation community.

responses.point: Perovskites are a remarkable materials-chemistry advance, but attribution is contested, since Kojima is absent from the credit list and Grätzel, Seok and Kanatzidis also contributed. Linke ranks targeted protein degradation first.
responses.response: I agree about Kojima and the crowding, and it is the main reason I hold my preference with some reservation. I would still defend Miyasaka, Park and Snaith as the most defensible trio, because they mark three distinct steps: first perovskite sensitiser, first solid-state device and first thin-film planar architecture. On B020 I think your Crews, Deshaies and Handa trio is chemically strong but leaves out Ciulli and the later molecular-glue chemistry. No degrader has yet been approved either, so I place it below perovskites on maturity, though I would support it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Targeted protein degradation is a genuine conceptual shift, but allocation between the PROTAC pioneers and the cereblon molecular-glue discoverers is unresolved, and Aili also notes perovskites are slightly early because stability is unresolved.
responses.response: We largely agree on the facts and differ on weighting. The PROTAC versus glue split you describe is the same kind of problem I have with perovskites, which makes me doubt B020 is a cleaner prize. I would only favour it if the committee accepts a two-name or Crews-Deshaies-Handa configuration. On timing, I think confirmed reproducibility counts for more than approvals pending.

responses.point: Base editing is a clearly defined chemical tool with Liu as intellectual leader, now clinically validated, and so ranks first.
responses.response: I ranked base editing fifth, and the reason is that it is a deaminase fused to a programmable binder, which is a modification of the genome editing already recognised in 2020, so the novelty is smaller than for a new material class. I agree that Liu is the clear leader and attribution is cleaner than for perovskites. I would keep it as an alternative, but if the committee wants to honour a single person, I would not argue against it.

uncertainties: Whether any three-person selection from the six credited perovskite names, and the omission of Kojima, can be defended as fair to Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis
Whether long-term stability and lead toxicity are seen as a maturity concern or only as an engineering matter
Whether the committee prefers a conceptually cleaner but narrower B047 or B020 over a broad materials topic with disputed credit
I have not independently verified the priority details of the 2009 to 2012 perovskite papers
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred B007 or the alternatives B020 and B047. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski, who ranks nitrogenase (B028) first, and I would not vote on that basis. My own field of electron crystallography (3D electron diffraction) touches porous materials rather than any shortlisted topic.
